bull.b: Record IET remaining performance obligations and a book-to-bill ratio well above one provide substantial revenue visibility beyond the current quarter. This backlog supports planning, utilization and recurring service opportunities, while confirming durable demand across LNG, gas infrastructure, power and industrial applications.

Healthy profitability combined with substantial operating and free cash flow indicates that reported earnings are converting into internally generated funds. This supports investment, integration spending and debt reduction, giving Baker Hughes greater capacity to fund its installed base and pursue growth without relying solely on external capital.

The Chart combination broadens Baker Hughes beyond traditional upstream activity into cryogenic storage, heat exchangers, carbon capture and industrial infrastructure. Strong data center demand adds another structural growth avenue, while cross-selling and cost synergies could improve the durability and mix of future revenue.

bear.b: The Chart acquisition materially increased leverage, reducing financial flexibility and raising interest expense while debt remains elevated relative to operating cash flow. Management plans to deleverage, but until that occurs, balance-sheet demands may constrain capital allocation and make the company more exposed to execution or demand setbacks.

Baker Hughes remains exposed to customer spending on upstream activity through OFSE, where a broadly flat 2026 spending environment limits near-term industry expansion. The year-over-year OFSE EBITDA decline also shows that IET growth and portfolio benefits may need to offset pressure in this established business.

A growing mix of longer-cycle projects can delay conversion of strong bookings into reported revenue and cash generation, making growth less immediate and execution more complex. Project timing, mix and inflation have already pressured IET margins, creating uncertainty around how quickly backlog translates into expanding profitability.
